text: ITIL 4 defines value as the perceived benefits, usefulness, and importance of something. Notice the word perceived — it's the consumer who decides whether value was created, not the provider who built the thing. A beautifully engineered workflow that nobody asked for, and that doesn't solve anyone's real problem, delivers almost no value no matter how clever the engineering behind it is. That's why Focus on Value is listed first among the seven guiding principles — every other principle exists to serve this one.

In practice, this principle collapses into one recurring question: how does this benefit the service consumer? Ask it before adding a new field to an intake form, before writing a new metric into a dashboard, before scheduling yet another recurring status meeting. If a report has been generated every single week for three years and nobody actually opens it, it isn't creating value — it's consuming it, in the time and effort it takes someone to keep producing it. This isn't a one-time audit. It's a habit applied constantly, at every point in the organization's work.

A single service interaction can create different value for different stakeholders at the exact same time. Resolving a laptop issue quickly creates value for the employee, who gets back to productive work. It creates value for that employee's manager, whose team's output stays protected. And it creates value for the business overall, in the form of steady productivity. These perspectives don't always line up neatly — something fast for the employee might be expensive for the provider to deliver — and Focus on Value asks IT to hold all of these views at once, not just the one that's easiest to measure.

This is exactly why Focus on Value comes before the other six guiding principles you'll meet in this chapter. Starting where you are, progressing iteratively, keeping things simple — those are all methods, ways of approaching work. Focus on Value is the purpose those methods are supposed to serve. A team can apply every other principle with real discipline and still build something polished that nobody actually needed, if they lose sight of who the output is ultimately for.

Value, defined by the consumer, checked constantly rather than assumed. Next up: the second guiding principle, Start Where You Are — why you assess what already exists before you decide to redesign it.
